To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

high glucose induces COX-2 expression via PKC-dependent generation of ROS, which in turn reduces NO availability and leads to an increase in the production of thromboxane, an endothelium-derived contracting factor.
glucose-induced activation of PKCs results in the formation of ROS and nitration of PGE2 synthase.
glucose causes upregulation of cyclooxygenase- 2 (COX-2) and alters prostanoid profile in human endothelial cells via protein kinase C (PKC) and reactive oxygen species (ROS).
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of cyclooxygenases (COX) in the pathogenesis of diabetic endothelial dysfunction.
the role of oxidative stress and cyclooxygenase-1 (COX-1) and COX-2 in the pathogenesis of diabetic endothelial dysfunction.
the effects of high glucose on the endothelial cell function.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
high glucose causes oxidative stress, which in turn activates PKC, which in turn upregulates COX-2 expression, which in turn leads to reduced availability of PGI2.
the increased COX-2 activity in the diabetic endothelium may contribute to endothelial dysfunction by reducing NO availability and increasing the formation of vasoconstrictive prostanoids.
hyperglycemia induces endothelial dysfunction via PKC-dependent activation of COX- 2 and NAD(P) H oxidase and that these effects are independent of each other.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
high glucose, via protein kinase C signaling, induces upregulation of cyclooxygenase- 2, resulting in altered prostanoid release and oxidative stress.
high glucose, via activation of PKC and formation of reactive oxygen species, upregulates COX-2 expression and causes alterations of the prostanoid profile and endothelial dysfunction.
glucose-induced oxidative stress is mediated via PKC-dependent activation of NAD(PH) oxidase.
The main takeaway from our work is that

high glucose, through activation of the PKC pathway and generation of ROS, causes a shift in the balance of endothelial-derived prostanoids, which may contribute to endothelial dysfunction in diabetic patients.
